question: `var mug = new Product("Mug", 9.50m); var pen = new Product("Pen", 1.25m);` Then `mug.Discount(10)` lowers the price of `mug`. What is the price of `pen` now?
options: `1.25m`, because each object made with `new` has its own instance data
`1.125m`, because a method called on one object of a class runs on every object of it
`9.50m`, because `pen` was created after `mug` and copied its values
It depends on the order the objects were created in
explanation: `new` creates a separate object each time, and `Discount` changes the price of the object it is called on, `mug`. `pen` keeps `1.25m`. The tempting answer describes a `static` member, which belongs to the class and is shared; instance members are not. Objects never copy each other's values just because they share a class.

question: A class declares `private static decimal balance;`, and `Deposit` adds to it. Two accounts are created and 100 is deposited into the first one. What does the second account report?
options: `0`, because each account starts with its own balance of `0`
`100`, because a `static` field is one value shared by every account
`200`, because the deposit is applied once per account
The code does not compile, because an instance method cannot change a `static` field
explanation: A `static` field belongs to the class, so there is only one `balance` for the whole program, and every account reads the same value: 100. Starting at `0` per account is what an instance field (without `static`) would do. Instance methods may read and write static fields, so it compiles, which is why this bug survives until the numbers look wrong.

question: Which property declaration lets every piece of code read `Balance`, but only the methods of the class change it?
options: `public decimal Balance { get; set; }`
`private decimal Balance { get; set; }`
`public decimal Balance { get; private set; }`
`public decimal Balance;`
explanation: `{ get; private set; }` makes reading public and writing private to the class, so outside code gets a compile error when it assigns `Balance`. `{ get; set; }` lets anyone write it, which is the most tempting choice because it is the most common shape. `private` on the whole property hides reading too, and a public field has no access control at all.

question: `Product? found = Find("BAG");` returns `null` because no product matches. What does `Console.WriteLine(found.Name);` do?
options: It prints an empty line, because a missing object has empty properties
It prints `null`
The compiler refuses to build the program
It throws `NullReferenceException`, because there is no object to read `Name` from
explanation: `null` means the variable refers to no object, so reading a member through it throws `NullReferenceException` when the line runs. Printing an empty line is tempting, but there is no object whose `Name` could be empty. With nullable checks on, the compiler only warns about the possible `null` (02/02), it does not refuse to build. Check with `if (found is null)` first.

question: Why is `enum OrderStatus { Pending, Paid, Shipped }` a better type for an order's status than a `string`?
options: An enum takes less memory, which is its main reason to exist
A misspelled status such as `OrderStatus.Shiped` is a compile error, while the string `"Shiped"` is accepted and fails only later, if at all
An enum can hold any number of values added while the program runs
Strings cannot be compared in a `switch` statement, enums can
explanation: The compiler knows every name of an enum, so a typo stops the build, and code completion lists the valid choices. A string accepts any text, so `"Shiped"` is stored and silently matches nothing. An enum's set of names is fixed when you write the code, not at run time. A `switch` works on strings too; memory is not the reason to choose an enum.

question: A constructor is written as `public Product(string name) { name = name; }`, and the class has a field `private string name = "";`. What is the value of the field after `new Product("Mug")`?
options: `"Mug"`, because the constructor assigns it
`null`, because the constructor clears the field
`""`, because `name = name` assigns the parameter to itself and never touches the field
The program throws `InvalidOperationException` when the constructor runs
explanation: Inside the constructor, `name` means the parameter, so `name = name` copies the parameter onto itself; the compiler only warns. The field keeps its initial `""`. The tempting answer `"Mug"` is what the line was meant to do. Write `this.name = name`, or call the field `_name` so the two names never collide.
